stories.topic: The Life Lessons Meetup in Goa
stories.summary: After three 2025 cohorts of their course Life Lessons (about 130 participants), Amit and Ajay held an in-person meetup in Goa. They hoped for 20 to 30 people. Between 50 and 60 came, each paying for their own flights and hotel, with last-minute arrivals from Thailand and New York driven by FOMO in the WhatsApp group. At the first lunch, the first seven people to sit with Amit were all on sabbatical. Amit calls himself a socially awkward introvert who dislikes crowds, yet this was the one gathering where he felt at ease with everyone. He credits a selection effect: a premium price and serious content attracted curious people with agency who weren't on the beaten path.
stories.insight: Price and effort act as filters. A high bar can select for exactly the community you want, and the internet lets us build communities of choice instead of living only within communities of circumstance.
stories.quote: this was the only gathering in my life where I just felt immediately at ease and comfortable with each and every person.

stories.summary: Alfred Kinsey put 521 questions to thousands of respondents and published books on male (1948) and female (1953) sexuality. He found that about a third of men admitted a homosexual experience, and that many women masturbated, thought about sex, and had partners beyond their husbands. The female volume proved too much even for America. The Rockefeller Foundation dropped his funding, he was ostracised, and he died of pneumonia at 62. Amit compares him to Ignaz Semmelweis, who showed that hand-washing before surgery saves lives, was ignored, and died in a lunatic asylum. Amit also flags Kinsey's limitation: his sample came from elite Westernised society and recorded stated rather than revealed preferences.
stories.insight: People who state uncomfortable truths are often punished in their lifetimes and vindicated so completely later that their treatment looks absurd. The obvious truths of tomorrow are often the taboos of today.
stories.quote: he was right so trivially that today it boggles the mind that he was treated the way he was.

stories.summary: Around 2006–07, an adult comic called Savita Bhabhi was becoming popular. Amit was then running his hugely popular blog India Uncut, about 8,000 posts in five years, roughly five a day. He blogged about the comic and likes to think he helped it go viral in the pre-Twitter era. One day he opened a new edition and found Savita Bhabhi discussing her favourite blog: India Uncut. Ajay introduced the tale as 'one of the highlights of Amit Varma's life.'
stories.insight: A funny snapshot of how things went viral before social media, when bloggers and underground comics fed each other's popularity, told with Amit's self-mocking pride.
stories.quote: one day I opened the latest edition of Savita Bhabhi to find that Savita Bhabhi is talking about her favorite blog and it is India Uncut. So what greater achievement could there be, Ajay Shah?

stories.topic: Women Who Hunted Osama bin Laden
stories.summary: Amit described the 'Miss Marple's Detective Agency' in women's minds: strong memory, attention to detail, relentless information-gathering. Ajay pointed out that we picture intelligence operatives as men out of John le Carré novels or James Bond films, yet these traits suit intelligence work perfectly. Critical people in the CIA's hunt for Osama bin Laden were women who could hold vast databases in their heads and spot the one thing that broke the pattern. He suggested India's intelligence services be rebuilt with many more women. Amit stressed that although it sounded glib, they both meant it seriously.
stories.insight: Our mental image of who suits a job is often shaped by fiction, not by the traits the job actually needs. Hiring for the real cognitive demands can reveal talent that stereotypes hide.
stories.quote: They had that ability to hold vast databases in their head and see one thing falling out of pattern.

stories.topic: Ovulation, Lap Dancers and Unconscious Signals
stories.summary: At the Goa meetup Amit joked that he would 'mansplain ovulation'. The finding he shared: during ovulation, women, whether they know it or not, tend to dress more revealingly, behave more sexily and be more open to 'bad boy' types. A study of lap dancers found that ovulating dancers earned by far the highest tips, then dancers who were neither ovulating nor menstruating, then menstruating dancers. It is unclear whether the women behaved differently or the men picked up on something. Even more striking, men became more protective of their partners during ovulation despite having no conscious way to know it was happening. In a separate blind smell test, the men women found sexiest by body odour turned out to be the most dominant and high-status.
stories.insight: A great deal of mating behaviour runs on signals that neither sender nor receiver consciously perceives. Our bodies are negotiating beneath our awareness.
stories.quote: So there is something happening at a subliminal instinctive level which we are not even aware of that our bodies are hardwired in all of these different ways.

recommendations.creator: Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam
recommendations.context: The book the whole episode is built around. Amit calls it an episode about a book, in the tradition of their earlier book episodes. It uses anonymised internet data (porn searches, romance-novel readership) to map what people actually want, then explains it with natural selection, psychology and sociology.
recommendations.reason: It moves beyond Kinsey's stated preferences to revealed preferences. Amit underlined nearly every page and says it made things he knew intuitively 'high definition' and showed him phenomena he had never considered. He especially loved the chapter on homosexuality. Ajay closed by urging readers to read it, because much of it is uncomfortable and departs from mainstream narratives.

recommendations.item: Sexual Behavior in the Human Male
recommendations.creator: Alfred Kinsey & others
recommendations.context: Kinsey's 1948 report, presented as the starting point for understanding the 'what' of human sexuality.
recommendations.reason: It blew apart myths of its time, for instance showing that about a third of men admitted a homosexual experience. Amit notes its limits: an elite Western sample and self-reported preferences.

recommendations.item: Sexual Behavior in the Human Female
recommendations.creator: Alfred Kinsey & others
recommendations.context: Kinsey's 1953 companion volume, which cost him his Rockefeller funding.
recommendations.reason: It showed that women have rich sexual lives (masturbation, fantasy, partners beyond their husbands), overturning the belief that sexuality was mainly a male thing.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Cited as the 1975 landmark that brought natural selection to a mass audience.
recommendations.reason: Essential background for the 'why' of sexuality. Amit cautions that the 'selfish gene' is a metaphor and should not be read literally.

recommendations.creator: Donald Symons
recommendations.context: Amit calls this 1979 book the second big milestone in popular evolutionary writing after Dawkins.
recommendations.reason: It used natural selection to explain why men and women are wired differently, and it set off a flood of later books on the subject, including A Billion Wicked Thoughts.

recommendations.creator: Steven Pinker
recommendations.context: The book through which Amit first discovered natural selection in the early 2000s.
recommendations.reason: It opened his eyes to how biology shapes us. He also cites Pinker's argument there that art and culture may be male ornamentation.

recommendations.creator: Geoffrey Miller
recommendations.context: One of the books Amit read that continued Symons's work.
recommendations.reason: Part of the group of books that showed him how biology works on human desire, and on his reading list for this subject.

recommendations.creator: David Buss
recommendations.context: Another of the post-Symons books Amit read and 'thoroughly enjoyed'.
recommendations.reason: It builds the evolutionary account of why men and women want what they want, which forms the shared ground this episode starts from.

recommendations.creator: Robert Wright
recommendations.context: Cited while discussing romance and jealousy as evolutionary adaptations.
recommendations.reason: Wright shows how the same impulses can produce different equilibria, with both monogamy and polygamy as logical adaptations depending on a society's direction. Amit leaves those 'fascinating' explanations for readers to discover.

recommendations.creator: Catherine Salmon and Donald Symons
recommendations.context: Source of the quotes Amit uses to frame the episode's headline finding: men are visual, women want stories.
recommendations.reason: It contrasts the male fantasy world of 'pornotopia' (lust without courtship) with the romance novel, which it reads as a chronicle of female mate choice.

recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for the first caveat Amit gives before the findings.
recommendations.reason: Hume's point that you cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is' guards against reading evolutionary explanations as moral justifications.

recommendations.creator: Wikipedia
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes for the second caveat.
recommendations.reason: G. E. Moore's fallacy of equating 'natural' with 'good' was once used by bigots against homosexuality. Something being natural makes it neither good nor bad.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: This episode began as a bonus session at the Life Lessons meetup in Goa. The course includes Ajay's detailed webinar on natural selection and a finance webinar.
recommendations.reason: Amit describes content and a community you won't find elsewhere: curious people with agency, plus a lively WhatsApp group he says you're 'missing out' on.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything Ep 125: Understanding Evolution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The show notes recommend it as a prelude. Amit refers back to it repeatedly, for example Ajay's springbok example of sexual versus natural selection and the is-ought fallacy.
recommendations.reason: It lays the natural-selection groundwork that this episode's 'why' of sexuality depends on.

core_ideas.concept: Communities of Circumstance vs Communities of Choice
core_ideas.explanation: For most of history your friends were set by geography: where you went to school and where you worked. The internet let Amit's 'cusp generation' form communities around shared interests instead. Almost all his close friends now come from such communities, and Life Lessons amplifies that.
core_ideas.quote: I am extremely lucky to be on that cusp generation which managed to move from communities of circumstance to communities of choice.

core_ideas.concept: Why Understanding Sexuality Matters
core_ideas.explanation: Amit gives four reasons. (1) Know thyself: otherwise we gaslight ourselves about our own urges. You must know yourself before you can be kind to yourself, and be kind to yourself before you can be kind to others. (2) Know others: we wrongly assume others share our instincts and judge them by our own standards. (3) It builds agency and compassion: knowing our wiring lets us override it, as Amit and Ajay did by choosing not to have kids despite the hardwired urge. (4) Mismatch: instincts built for hunter-gatherer scarcity misfire in a world of porn, dating apps and birth control.
core_ideas.quote: I believe understanding human nature increases both our agency and our compassion.

core_ideas.concept: Is-Ought and the Naturalistic Fallacy
core_ideas.explanation: Two guardrails. Hume's is-ought problem: 'men are wired to be promiscuous' does not imply they should be, just as being hardwired for violence doesn't justify violence. G. E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy is the reverse error of treating natural as good. Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and therefore bad, which is wrong on both counts, since it is perfectly natural in our species and many others.
core_ideas.quote: You do not get to an ought from an is.

core_ideas.concept: Proximate vs Ultimate Causation
core_ideas.explanation: We crave sweets because, when calories were unpredictable, people who stocked up survived and passed on their genes. We dislike bitterness because poisonous plants taste bitter. That is the ultimate cause. The proximate cause is simply 'I like it.' Evolutionary explanations describe why instincts were shaped hundreds of thousands of years ago, not what anyone consciously thinks today.
core_ideas.quote: he likes a rasgulla today because he just does. That's a proximate reason for it. But the ultimate causation is of the genes.

core_ideas.concept: Averages Are Not Identities (The Shoe-Size Analogy)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's statistical intuition: on average older kids have bigger feet, but not every older child has bigger feet than every younger one, and five-year-olds vary hugely among themselves. A real correlation has explanatory power while leaving lots of individual variation. Generalisations about men and women work the same way.
core_ideas.quote: So on average, something can be true, but that's not our essential identity.

core_ideas.concept: The Root Asymmetry: Promiscuous Men, Selective Women
core_ideas.explanation: In ancestral conditions, spreading genes cost a man almost nothing, while a woman paid with pregnancy and years of child-rearing and got few 'shots'. So men evolved to seek quantity, and women to be selective in two ways: good genes (dominant, high-status men whose sons will also spread genes) and a reliable provider who helps the child survive. From this follow men's attraction to youth and beauty (present and future fertility, health) and women's attraction to status and power. Amit says nearly every male–female difference flows from this asymmetry, and it is description, not prescription.
core_ideas.quote: Men are wired to be promiscuous, women are wired to be selective.

core_ideas.concept: Ornamentation: Signals Built for Sexual Selection
core_ideas.explanation: Ornaments like the peacock's tail or a springbok's high jump help an animal get mates even if they make it easier for predators to spot, so there is an optimal trade-off between the two pressures. In humans, beauty works as a health signal. Ideal female faces differ across cultures but are all symmetrical, and symmetry and clear skin both indicate good health.
core_ideas.quote: We find symmetry beautiful because it is a sign of good health.

core_ideas.concept: What Men's Searches Reveal: Fertility Cues
core_ideas.explanation: Revealed preferences (what men search for, not what they say they want) point to youth and fertility. 'Teenage' is the top search term. Searches for 'fat' outnumber 'skinny' three to one, which suggests the skinny ideal comes from women's magazines like Vogue and Cosmopolitan rather than from men. Men prefer a 0.7 waist-to-hip ratio without ever searching for hips. In a British bar experiment, a woman got hit on far more as padding took her from an A cup to a C cup. Big breasts, big butts and small feet form one cluster, because healthy estrogen levels produce gynoid fat and small feet.
core_ideas.quote: our instincts are hardwired in such a way that we are drawn to these signs of fertility and therefore we are just drawn to these areas of the human body without ever actually knowing why.

core_ideas.concept: When the Cue Matters More Than the Woman
core_ideas.explanation: Visual triggers can work almost independently of any actual partner. About half of roosters tried to mate with a fake hen's head on a feathered board, and turkeys will try with a rubber ball at the right height. Hentai exploits the same logic by exaggerating every cue.
core_ideas.quote: About half of all roosters attempted copulation with an artificial chicken head mounted on a feather covered board.

core_ideas.concept: Visual Men, Narrative Women
core_ideas.explanation: The book's headline finding. Men respond to images and women to stories. At the time of writing, about 2% of credit-card payments for porn came from women, while about 90% of romance novels are read by women, and romance is by far the largest fiction genre. A brief clip can be enough for a man, while the female equivalent is a whole novel.
core_ideas.quote: a sixty second Pornhub clip of a woman unbuttoning her shirt can compel a man to masturbate to ejaculation. But the single most popular artifact used by women to generate arousal takes the form of a two fifty page book that requires hours to digest.

core_ideas.concept: Miss Marple's Detective Agency
core_ideas.explanation: Ogas and Gaddam's metaphor: every woman's mind runs four detectives (social, cultural, emotional and physical) to vet potential mates, while men have only the physical one. This helps explain why women tend to remember more, talk and text more, and build networks of 'informants'. The downside is higher rates of anxiety, depression and eating disorders, because the detective work never stops. Amit has learned to seek advice from women close to him when he's stuck on 'male hardware issues'.
core_ideas.quote: They use conversation for connection, not information.

core_ideas.concept: Physical vs Psychological Arousal
core_ideas.explanation: In men, physical and psychological arousal go together. In women they are separate processes in different parts of the brain. In one study, women showed physical arousal to almost every image, including gorillas mating, but psychological arousal to only one or two, while men's bodies didn't respond to the gorillas at all. A critical consequence: a woman's body may respond during rape, but that is not consent or secret enjoyment.
core_ideas.quote: These are deeply separate processes in women.

core_ideas.concept: The Power of Or vs the Power of And
core_ideas.explanation: Male arousal works on 'or': any one cue, whether breasts, a butt or simple willingness, can be enough. Female arousal works on 'and': looks, conversation, attentiveness, status ('is he a chauffeur or a CEO?') and more all have to line up. That is why turning on a man is easy and turning on a woman is hard. Amit rejects the advice books telling women to 'settle'.
core_ideas.quote: So it's the power of or. But women are much more selective, so it's the power of and.

core_ideas.concept: Romance Novels as Women's Revealed Preferences
core_ideas.explanation: Just as porn reveals male preferences, romance novels reveal female ones. Heroes tend to be dominant, even obnoxious, which helps explain why serial killers attract female admirers. The core fantasy is 'taming the wild coconut': a cad who is hard outside and soft inside, whom the heroine alone domesticates, often bringing him to tears. Status matters enormously too.
core_ideas.quote: In the romance titles on Amazon, there are four hundred and fifteen millionaires, two eighty six billionaires, and two sixty three sheikhs

core_ideas.concept: The Two Great Self-Delusions
core_ideas.explanation: Each sex has a typical fantasy. The female one is that the exciting bad boy and the steady provider can be found in one man, which romance novels endlessly sell even though few people are both. The male one is that he can reliably give a woman sexual satisfaction, which is often untrue and leads women to fake it to please men.
core_ideas.quote: the great self delusion for women is that they can get both the men in one body.

core_ideas.concept: Romance, Jealousy and Their Asymmetry
core_ideas.explanation: Romance and jealousy are adaptations that keep parents together long enough to raise children. Male jealousy is sexual because a man doesn't want to raise another man's child. Female jealousy is emotional because a woman needs commitment and provision. Amit says this, alongside patriarchy and social conditioning, partly explains why wives forgive infidelity more often than husbands do.
core_ideas.quote: male jealousy is always physical jealousy, sexual jealousy, right? Whereas female jealousy is emotional jealousy.

core_ideas.concept: Men Are Smart Because Women Are Selective
core_ideas.explanation: In many species, such as dragonflies, females aren't choosy. Human females are, so men must compete, and male intelligence and displays become ornaments. Pinker suggests in The Blank Slate that art and culture may be male ornamentation.
core_ideas.quote: In humans, men are smart because women are selective.

core_ideas.concept: Women Want to Be Lovable, Men Aspire to Greatness
core_ideas.explanation: Being lovable secures commitment and is relatively achievable. Men compete in a winner-take-most game: Amit's rough recollection is that about 80% of women but about 30% of men have descendants, and dating apps make it worse. So men take mad risks (the 'dumb ways to die' accounts are nearly all men) and chase greatness. Amit calls that chase toxic and an obstacle to happiness, a hardwired trait to recognise and resist. Men should also aspire to be lovable.
core_ideas.quote: Women want to be lovable, men aspire for greatness.

core_ideas.concept: Gay Men Have Male Brains
core_ideas.explanation: Gay men's desire works like straight men's: visual, focused on the same body zones, with little interest in story. They often prefer straight porn because they are drawn to macho, actually-straight men. That gave rise to 'straight porn for gay men', which focuses the camera on the man, and women started watching it too because they finally got to look at the man.
core_ideas.quote: the brains of gay males are wired exactly like that of straight males, in the sense that it's visual dominated.

core_ideas.concept: Madame de Staël's Asymmetry of Desire
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing line, which he thinks sits at the heart of human sexuality. Men's desire points at women, while women's desire is for being desired. He suggests much modern behaviour and social complexity follows from this.
core_ideas.quote: The desire of the man is for the woman. The desire of the woman is for the desire of the man.

core_ideas.concept: Hardwiring Is Not Destiny: The Project of Civilisation
core_ideas.explanation: Nature and nurture interact rather than one ruling. Knowing our wiring, rather than denying it, is what lets us choose otherwise and live by values we pick. Ajay adds that modern social-media culture, in peculiar ways, enforces very old-fashioned sexual inhibitions even more toxically than traditional society did.
core_ideas.quote: Sometimes nurture amplifies nature, sometimes it mitigates nature, which is to my mind the project of civilization, to mitigate the worst instincts of our hard wiring and choose who we want to be and live accordingly.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: On presenting the sexuality session at Goa, Amit was 'at pains to give the caveat to everyone present that this is not a practical class, but theory, theory.'

After Ajay's lesson on averages, Amit's WhatsApp joke: 'On Life Lessons, everybody reads an average of one paper a day. But what's really happening is 139 of us don't read papers at all, and Ajay Shah reads 140 papers every night.' Ajay corrects him: 'I'm averaging three papers a week.'
Amit on his violent instincts: 'in traffic I become a Punjabi, otherwise I'm fully Bengali.'

Amit, tripping over 'who they are, who be them': 'Who says who be them? Gentle readers, I'm sorry, we are growing old. Enjoy these episodes while they last, we'll be a babbling mess in a scant few weeks.'
Amit, on the comic's visiting tailors: 'I like to tell people I'm a trained ladies tailor, which is not true in the tailoring aspect of it.'
Amit's naughty rewrite of 'My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean' (once covered by the Beatles), in honour of the voluptuous Bengali boudi: 'My Boudi Lies Over the Lotion.'

Ajay notes that porn thrived even on weak 640x480 screens and was 'always the pioneering app that drove computer usage'. Amit recalls dial-up days when 'Samantha Fox is half done, she's at the neck and you're waiting for the rest to come.'

Amit's CEO joke, from their friend Narendra Shenoy: a CEO gives each of three girlfriends a million dollars. One beautifies herself, one buys him a Sony FX3 and XM4 headphones, and one invests in diversified index funds 'just as you recommend in our finance webinar' and turns it into three million. 'Who does he choose? He chooses the one with the big boobs.' Ajay: 'I didn't see that coming.' Amit: 'I'm glad it came.'
Amit before his Goa talk: 'ladies, I'm gonna go up there and I'm gonna mansplain to you about ovulation.'
After learning that male intelligence is an ornament, Amit's new line for women: 'if you think I'm smart, it's because of you... It's my peacock's tail.'

Amit, on the rarity of combining cad and provider: 'seldom can everyone combine the sexual allure of the younger Ajay Shah and the responsible vibe of the older Ajay Shah. Or would you say you combine both of them now... let's not embarrass you.'

Amit: 'Ajay Shah, you're so lovable. Is this intentional or are you just naturally a little woman?' Ajay: 'I'm fifty-nine years old. I grew up.' Amit: 'Nobody grows up... There are no adults... Adulting is the biggest con job that they tell you.'
Ajay's 'pretty line': 'Men love women, women love children, children love kittens.' Amit: 'There is no reciprocity.'
Ogas and Gaddam's opening observation that we understand our sexuality poorly: 'Scientists have an easier time gazing at intergalactic quasars than peeking into someone's bedroom.'
'Know thyself', the inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, together with Socrates's 'the unexamined life is not worth living', as Amit's first reason for studying sexuality.
Donald Symons: 'To encounter erotica designed to appeal to the other sex is to gaze into the psychological abyss that separates the sexes.'
Steven Pinker's line, roughly, that 'nature gives us knobs, nurture turns them', used to dismiss the nature-versus-nurture binary.

Internet Rule 34, 'there is porn of it', for the long tail of desire. Amit begs that there be no Tom and Jerry porn, and notes that despite the long tail, about 20 search terms account for about 80% of searches.
Charles Sobhraj, who committed many murders yet was always picking up women, cited as evidence of the hardwired pull of dominant 'bindaas' bad men.

Neil Strauss's The Game, which Amit calls 'perhaps the earliest handbook for incels': 'You don't have to be an asshole, but if you have no choice, being an inconsiderate asshole beats being a polite beta every time.'

The Flame and the Flower, Amit's quiz question for Ajay: the first romance novel published straight to paperback, which made the genre explode. It opens with the hero raping the heroine, whom she later 'tames', the classic wild-coconut arc.
Amit places this as a 'book episode', following their earlier episodes on Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson and James C. Scott's Seeing Like a State.
